content: Decreased levels of nitric oxide have been suggested as a potential cellular mechanism contributing to the development of necrotising enterocolitis (NEC). Arginine serves as a precursor for nitric oxide synthesis in tissues, and supplementation with arginine may help prevent NEC in preterm infants. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of arginine supplementation, administered through any route, on the incidence of NEC in preterm neonates. Subgroup analyses were planned based on the dosage of arginine and the gestational age of the infants (≤ 32 weeks or > 32 weeks). A comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's standard strategy. Databases searched included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL, covering studies up to May 12, 2016. Additional sources such as clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed to identify randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomised trials. The inclusion criteria were RCTs and quasi-randomised trials comparing arginine supplementation (administered orally or parenterally for at least seven days) with placebo or no treatment. This supplementation was in addition to any enteral or parenteral nutrition the infant was already receiving. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using information from study reports and direct communication with the authors. Data on relevant outcomes were extracted, and effect sizes were calculated as risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and mean differences (MD), as appropriate. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Three eligible studies were identified, involving a total of 285 neonates, of whom 140 received arginine supplementation. These studies were conducted in three different countries. The overall methodological quality of the studies was deemed good. A statistically significant reduction in the risk of developing NEC (any stage) was observed in the arginine group compared to the placebo group (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.64; I² = 27%). The risk difference was ‐0.19 (95% CI ‐0.28 to ‐0.10; I² = 0%), and the quality of evidence was rated as moderate. The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one case of NEC was six (95% CI 4 to 10). Further analysis revealed a significant reduction in the risk of NEC stage 1 (RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.90; I² = 52%) and NEC stage 3 (RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.03; I² = 0%) in the arginine group compared to the control group. The risk differences for these stages were ‐0.07 (95% CI ‐0.14 to ‐0.01; I² = 0%) and ‐0.05 (95% CI ‐0.09 to ‐0.01; I² = 89%), respectively. The quality of evidence for these findings was also moderate. Arginine supplementation was associated with a significant reduction in NEC-related mortality (RR 0.18, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.00; I² = 0%), with a risk difference of ‐0.05 (95% CI ‐0.09 to ‐0.01; I² = 87%). However, there was clinical heterogeneity in mortality rates. Mortality from any cause did not differ significantly between the arginine and control groups (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.45; I² = 42%), with a risk difference of ‐0.03 (95% CI ‐0.10 to 0.04; I² = 79%). No significant adverse effects directly attributable to arginine supplementation were reported, including hypotension or disturbances in glucose homeostasis. Follow-up data from one trial showed no statistically significant differences in long-term adverse outcomes, such as cerebral palsy, cognitive delay, bilateral blindness, or hearing loss requiring hearing aids, at 36 months of age. The findings are limited by the relatively small sample size of the included studies. The authors concluded that arginine supplementation may help prevent NEC in preterm infants. However, due to the limited data from three small trials involving 285 participants, the evidence is insufficient to support a definitive clinical recommendation. A larger, multi-centre randomised controlled trial focusing on the incidence of NEC, particularly at more severe stages (2 and 3), is necessary to confirm these findings.
